title: Predestination
hookLine: Calvin and the Reformed stress God's sovereign choosing; they find comfort in it

lines: YOUR ONLY COMFORT IN LIFE AND DEATH?
A COLD WORD, OR A WARM ONE?
cards: What is your only comfort in life and in death? That's the first question of the Heidelberg Catechism, a teaching book of the Reformed churches, and children in some Reformed congregations learn it by heart.
The answer, put simply: that I am not my own, but belong, body and soul, to my faithful Savior Jesus Christ. Notice the word at the heart of the question. Comfort.
Not argument, not fear. Some people hear today's word as cold, even frightening. The people who hold it closest speak of it as comfort.

teach.h: PREDESTINATE: THE WORD IS IN ROMANS.
teach.b: The word is in the Bible. Paul writes in Romans: "For whom he did foreknow, he also did predestinate to be conformed to the image of his Son."

And in Ephesians: "he hath chosen us in him before the foundation of the world." Yesterday, Augustine said grace must come first. John Calvin and the Reformed churches after him followed that line all the way back.

If grace comes first, they said, then before any of us chose God, God chose us. Salvation rests on God's choosing, not on our deciding well. They call this God's sovereignty: God is God, and God's purposes don't fail.
Here's where the warmth comes in: Reformed Christians speak of this as comfort. If my hold on God depended on me, they say, it would be as shaky as I am on a bad day.
If it depends on God's choosing, it's as steady as God. Jesus says of his sheep, in John's Gospel: "neither shall any man pluck them out of my hand."
Not a ladder you have to keep climbing, but a hand that won't let go.
The doctrine raises hard questions, and Reformed teachers admit it: what about those not chosen? Some answer with humility, and leave the question with God.
Other Christians answer it differently, and tomorrow we'll hear them. This week, then: a dance, a world from nothing, a fossil, an image, a wound, an argument about grace, and now a hand.
Seven ways of asking who God is, and who we are.

how: Reformed and Presbyterian churches teach predestination in their confessions and catechisms, and some members learn the Heidelberg Catechism's first question and answer, on comfort in life and death, by heart.

s: the word predestinate isn't in the Bible
it's in Romans 8, in the King James: whom he did foreknow, he also did predestinate.
Reformed Christians speak of predestination as a comfort
the Heidelberg Catechism begins with comfort: I belong to my faithful Savior. if salvation rests on God's choosing, it's as steady as God.
Calvin invented the idea that grace comes first
Augustine taught it long before him, against Pelagius. Calvin and the Reformed followed that line.

games.q: a Reformed friend tells you predestination is their deepest comfort. you ask why. what do they say?
o: because it means they can stop caring how they live.
because their hold on God rests on God's choosing, not their own steadiness.
because they know exactly who is chosen.
games.why: Reformed Christians say that if salvation depended on them, it would be as shaky as they are. resting on God's choosing, it's as steady as God.

practice: Sit back so the chair takes your whole weight, let your shoulders drop, and feel the floor holding you without any help from you. Notice how much effort you usually spend keeping yourself together, and set some of it down.
If you pray, rest in the line from John, neither shall any man pluck them out of my hand; if you don't, let the chair and the floor hold you, and let that be enough.

wordCard.voice: Predestination. God choosing before we choose. Calvin and the Reformed churches stress it, and they speak of it as a comfort: held by a hand that won't let go.

orig.note: Greek: to mark out beforehand. Paul's word in Romans 8:29, predestinate in the King James.

carryVoice: Your line: held by his choosing. For those who hold it, a comfort. Same time tomorrow.
